expansion: Iridodialysis, the separation of the iris root from the ciliary body, is the only option that directly produces monocular diplopia after trauma. The lecture marks this relationship on slide 29, stating “Iridodialysis — (UNIOCULAR DIPLOPIA)” (L25, slide 29). When the iris is torn away, an abnormal pupil edge creates a second pseudo‑pupil that splits the visual axis, giving the patient double vision in the affected eye. Iridodonesis, listed in option A, describes a trembling iris that oscillates with eye movements and is usually seen with lens subluxation; it does not generate an extra visual axis and therefore does not cause diplopia (not taken from the course material). Angle‑recession glaucoma, option C, is a late sequela of blunt trauma that raises intra‑ocular pressure and may produce visual field loss, but it is not associated with double vision (not taken from the course material). Uniocular hyphema, option D, is blood accumulating in the anterior chamber; the slides on hyphema (slides 25‑28) emphasize pain, reduced visual acuity and risk of raised IOP, but they never link it to diplopia (L25, slides 25‑28). Consequently, B is the only choice that matches the lecture content and the pathophysiology of post‑traumatic diplopia.
objective: Identify which post‑traumatic ocular condition can cause diplopia
